Short answer: inventory is updated when the returned items are actually received/processed by the warehouse — not merely when the return record is marked complete/approved. Make sure the “receive” step has been done for the return (or update the return before receiving) [7471112-2][7471112-5][73634379-15][73634379-17].

What to check/do
- Check the per-item return response type (Wait and Replace / Replace Immediately / Refund and Replace Immediately) — these determine whether the system expects the original item back and how the return is handled [7471112-2][7471112-4][7471112-5].  
- Ensure the warehouse has processed the physical return and set the item status to “received” (company receives and processes the items). Inventory changes occur when the company/warehouse processes the returned items as received [7471112-2][7471112-5].  
- If you need to change quantities on an existing return before receipt, use the Update Return flow (add/remove items or edit returnable qty) and then complete the Receive Sales Return step so inventory updates [73634379-17][73634379-15].

If after confirming the receive step inventory still hasn’t changed, re-run the “receive”/process-return action or check logs/transactions for the return processing (the docs describe the receive/process step as the inventory-affecting action) [7471112-2][7471112-5].

Pointers to get a quick breakthrough (from OFBiz docs):

- Check JVM heap and cache behavior: OFBiz uses SoftReferences for entity caches; if Xms/Xmx are too small the GC will repeatedly clear caches and slow things down. Set a reasonably large max heap (guideline ~75% of server RAM) and raise the initial heap (Xms) to avoid repeated heap growth/GC. Example production settings and Java requirement noted in the docs (eg. -Xms256M -Xmx2048M; OFBiz requires Java 17) [7045138-31].

- Inspect WebTools cache management for Soft Reference activity: frequent cache eviction there points to heap sizing problems [7045138-31].

- Database-heavy features need DB tuning: searches and other DB‑intensive ops rely on how the database handles queries — profile and tune those queries and the DB configuration [7045138-31]. Also monitor/maintain and clean the database (remove unimportant data) to reduce load [6553844-29].

- Do proper performance/load testing after customizations: custom code can dramatically change performance; always test after development to reproduce and isolate bottlenecks [6553844-92].

- Scale and architecture options: if single‑node tuning isn’t enough, consider running multiple OFBiz nodes behind a load balancer and follow architectural guidance for scaling beyond one instance [7045138-31].

- Watch background jobs and batch processes: long-running background tasks can dominate resources and need separate tuning, scheduling or resource allocation (real-world cases required lengthy tuning) [6553967-12].

- Operational checks: verify database health, clear/adjust distributed entity cache mechanisms where appropriate, and remove stale data to reduce work for OFBiz [6553844-29].

Start with JVM heap sizing and database-query profiling — those are the most common and highest‑impact fixes in the docs [7045138-31][6553844-29].

Short checklist of likely causes and what to verify in OFBiz (based on the OFBiz docs):

1. JDBC driver jar is installed where OFBiz expects it (entity/lib/jdbc). The docs explicitly advise copying the JDBC driver jar into entity/lib/jdbc for DB drivers (example shown for MS SQL). [71013152-16]

2. Datasource config: confirm your entityengine datasource uses an inline-jdbc entry with the driver class, full JDBC URI, username and password and reasonable pool settings (pool-minsize, pool-maxsize, etc.). The docs show inline-jdbc examples and the expected attributes (jdbc-driver, jdbc-uri, jdbc-username, jdbc-password, isolation-level, pool-minsize/pool-maxsize). Ensure values match your RDS endpoint, port and credentials. [71013152-14] [71013152-15] [71013152-16]

3. Delegator -> datasource mapping: verify the delegator group-map(s) point to the correct datasource name used by your inline-jdbc (e.g., group-map ... datasource-name="localpostgres"). If the delegator maps to a different datasource name, OFBiz will not use your RDS config. [71013152-19]

4. Enable/check connection verification at startup: use/check attributes like check-on-start (and review startup logs) so OFBiz reports connection failures early. The datasource examples include check-on-start and related attributes. [71013152-14] [71013152-15]

5. If OFBiz runs as a system service, ensure the service user owns the OFBiz tree and has the correct permissions and environment (JVM path, etc.). The service docs recommend running OFBiz under a dedicated user with ownership of the OFBiz install and editing the rc.ofbiz script variables accordingly. Permission or environment differences between your interactive Java test and the OFBiz service can cause connection failures. [6553871-2]

- Confirm the orders/shipments/invoices are marked as sales types. OFBiz automation (billing/auto-invoice/GL posting) is gated on sales types — e.g. auto-invoice fires only when shipment is SALES_SHIPMENT and auto-payment when order is SALES_ORDER. If the type is non‑sales, the triggers “simply never match” and you get no invoice/payment/accounting activity (so no commission run output) [430409055-3].

1. Open the invoice(s) and confirm they are a sales invoice (so the “find sales invoice for commission run” logic will include them) [71014328-1].

4. After correcting types/assignments, re-run the commission process so the invoices are discoverable by the commission run logic.

- This is by-design behavior of OFBiz automation: if the order/shipment/invoice are not sales-type, billing and downstream posting (including anything that depends on those postings such as commission runs) will not run — resulting in “no output” rather than an error. You must use sales-type entities for the ECAs to trigger [430409055-3][71014328-1].

Short answer: the failure is caused by the accounting GL post (createAcctgTransAndEntries → postAcctgTrans) throwing an exception and forcing the transaction to rollback. Two documented workarounds:

Short answer and action plan.

How to identify the leaking objects/code
- Profile the running application to find hotspots, high object-allocation counts and methods that retain objects; concentrate fixes where profiles show the most allocation/retention (profile for: allocated object counts, time spent in methods, call paths) [7045148-3].  
- Once you have the profiler output, inspect the code paths showing high allocations/retained objects (e.g., caches, loops creating many short‑lived objects) and fix by removing unintended retention or reusing/clearing structures [7045148-3].

GC / memory-setting suggestions
- OFBiz uses SoftReferences for many caches; when the JVM must grow the heap it runs GC and clears soft refs, so frequent heap growth will make caches appear to be “evaporating” or behaving oddly [7045138-31].  
- Avoid small initial heaps. Set a reasonably large initial heap (-Xms) and a sufficiently large max heap (-Xmx). Recommendation guidance: size max heap at roughly 75% of server RAM and make the initial heap high (even equal to max) to avoid repeated heap growth and soft-ref clearing. Example guidance shown: -Xms256M -Xmx2048M as a typical production pattern, adjusted to your server [7045138-31]. Also note OFBiz requires Java 17 or later for current versions [7045138-31].

Operational / scaling notes
- For very large read‑heavy data sets that won’t fit in memory, consider architecture changes (read replicas / multiple read‑only DBs or additional nodes) rather than forcing everything into memory [7766067-3].  
- Balance scalability vs. raw single‑instance performance when choosing fixes—optimize where real performance bottlenecks exist per profiling before broad changes [7766067-4].

Suggested short workflow
1. Run a profiler and capture allocation/retention and method hotspots [7045148-3].  
2. Fix the code paths holding references (clear caches, avoid long‑lived unnecessary collections).  
3. Increase/align JVM heap settings (-Xms/-Xmx) to reduce GC-triggered clearing of SoftReferences [7045138-31].  
4. If dataset still too big, evaluate scaling options (replicas / multiple nodes) [7766067-3].

References: profiling and allocation guidance [7045148-3]; SoftReference and heap/GC behaviour and heap sizing guidance [7045138-31]; scaling/read-replica suggestion [7766067-3]; scalability trade‑offs [7766067-4].

This can happen because invoicing/fulfillment and payment capture are separate steps in OFBiz:

- Invoices are created when the shipment is marked Packed; the system/Accountant sends the invoice and later associates received payments and marks invoices paid when money is actually received [7471143-0].

So an invoice can be moved forward while the payment remains in an uncaptured/received state if capture hasn’t happened or if the invoice was advanced/marked manually before the payment was associated. Summary — Service vs Event (OFBiz)

- Purpose: Events are for validations/conversions (map processor); Services are for business logic (CRUD) [184617942-34].
- Return type: Service => Map; Event => String [184617942-34].
- Definitions & loading: Services require a definition and are loaded with the server (changes to definitions need reload); Events do not require a definition [184617942-34].
- Implementation options: Services: entity-auto, Java, Simple (XML), Groovy; Events: Simple (XML), Java, Groovy [184617942-34].
- Invocation: You can call a service from an event, but not an event from a service [184617942-34].
- Scope/usage: Events are usually local/specific to a place; Services are reusable and callable by name from anywhere/network [184617942-34].
- HTTP/session access: Events have access to HttpServletRequest/HttpServletResponse (and session); Services only see service parameters (no request/session) [184617942-34].
- Scheduling: Services can be scheduled as jobs; events cannot [184617942-34].

- Services are invoked with an input map (runService/serviceName, inputMap) and expect particular parameter names; copying a value into the expected field name ensures the service receives it correctly [doc:framework/minilang/src/docs/asciidoc/minilang-to-groovy-manual.adoc-3].
- The ofbiz:service/ofbiz:param mechanism also maps IN parameters into the service input map and places OUT parameters into the chosen scope (resultTo) — so names matter for both IN and OUT mapping [50233686-9].
- The field-to-result behavior documents how service fields/results are mapped; using set ensures the right field is present for that mapping to work [6553867-16].

- Verify the service’s expected input parameter name(s) and that the <set> is copying into that exact name.
- Verify whether the value being passed is an encoded/key value vs. the actual persistent id the service or persistence layer expects; you must provide the value the service is coded to handle (decoding/conversion can be done before calling the service) [doc:framework/minilang/src/docs/asciidoc/minilang-to-groovy-manual.adoc-3] [50233686-9].
